extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. sources.title: Meta unveils camera-free AI Ray-Bans amid 'pervert glasses' backlash
passages: The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses.

Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras.
You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses.
Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses.
From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects.
Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses.
Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside.
Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

extraction.body: Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses. From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light, there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists, and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

sources.title: Meta's $1,300 VR Glasses Look Like The Vision Pro Sequel Apple Should Be Making - Engadget
passages: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.

Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

extraction.body: Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged. The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same. [Image: Here’s the compute puck. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands. Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers). Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds. Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser. Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio. Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity. The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds. Disclosure: Meta provided lodging for one Road to VR reporter to attend Meta Connect 2026 where information for this article was gathered .

And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).

On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames.

Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset.

Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.)

Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.

The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.

Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

extraction.body: Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged. The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same. [Image: Here’s the compute puck. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands. Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers). Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds. Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser. Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio. Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity. The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds. Disclosure: Meta provided lodging for one Road to VR reporter to attend Meta Connect 2026 where information for this article was gathered .

Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content.

While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S.

Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more.

Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot.

When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand.
Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there.

At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking.

Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser.

Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio.
Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity.

The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: Meta to release Muse Charm, a Tamagotchi-like device for the Muse AI agent
passages: Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses.At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant.
Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice.
Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record.
Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year.

sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: What To Expect At Meta Connect 2026: New AI Glasses, A Mixed Reality Headset And More - Engadget
passages: It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year.
Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors.
I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse .
More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses.
Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others.
In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect.

Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility.
The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote.
I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem.
Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 .
These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant.

Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover.

extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products.
Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries.

Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok.
It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves.
It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey.
Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads.
"We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut.

I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later.

Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications.

No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram.

The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram.
Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing.

In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge.
Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said.
However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet.
"For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character.
It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm.
"I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about.

And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point.
"Threads didn't bring anything new to the table.
No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram.

Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family.
This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads.
What is after all one year in the life of a digital product?
However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular.
"It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted.
Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

coreStoryFacts.text: It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year.
Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors.
I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse .
More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses.
Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others.
In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect.

Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility.
The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote.
I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem.
Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 .
These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant.

Meta says that today’s keynote by Mark Zuckerberg will be about how “Meta is building a future for everyone” — something he wrote at length about in a recent essay about AI, smart glasses, and more.

The company is dealing with an outpouring of privacy and harassment concerns stemming from the product line’s built-in camera, which has led to them being derided as “pervert glasses.” Meta has already tried to tackle that reputation with recent privacy fixes and a new marketing campaign, but it could introduce more updates on the Connect stage.
That means we can expect more news from Zuckerberg and his team on those topics; perhaps we’ll hear more about Meta’s recently launched Muse AI agent and new glasses hardware.

extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey.
Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads.
"We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut.

I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later.
