extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

story.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too

facts.text: Meta , led by CEO and AI enthusiast Mark Zuckerberg, this week rolled out the first photo and video tools to come out of its Superintelligence Labs: Muse Photo and Muse Video.

The tool brings Meta in line with the state of the art in AI media creation, alongside Google’s Gemini and Seedance 2.0, but along with the tools, Meta also said that all public Instagram profiles will be opt-out, not opt-in, and other users can pull in those other accounts that don’t opt out and create new content using their profiles.
We call on Meta to make protection the default on Muse Image, not the exception, and enable individuals to opt-in if they want to allow usage of their image or likeness for AI content creation.
Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”
Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.

This isn't a platform in which AI DJs take jobs away from Wolfman Jack or whatever.
Rather, it's a tool that lets people use natural conversation to describe the type of radio station they want to listen to.
The algorithm will take in that information and create some tailor-made radio.
This is sort of like Spotify's AI DJ from a while back , but the conversational element should make the algorithm zero in on your exact tastes as described.

extraction.body: YouTube Music today is making official sound search, while acknowledging that it’s testing the “AI-generated conversational radio” for US Premium subscribers. The Hum to Search-adjacent capability is called “sound search” in YouTube Music. It simply lets you query YTM’s “catalog of over 100 million official songs by sound.” Some users had it in May before the feature was rolled back for whatever reason. Once available, you can tap the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner of YouTube Music to access a waveform button. (It appears next to the existing microphone for voice search.) This launches a fullscreen UI that lets you sing, hum, or play a song. The results page shows cover art, song name, artist, album, year, and download status, as well as buttons to Play or Save to your library. The recognition can be quite fast. Sound search is rolling out to YouTube Music for Android and iOS starting today. Meanwhile, YouTube Music is confirming that it’s testing an “AI-generated conversational radio” in the US for Premium users. It lets you create a custom radio by “describing exactly what they want to hear.” Be on the lookout for the “Ask for music any way you like” card in your Home feed. This opens a chat-based UI with a field at the bottom that lets you “Ask for music.” Considered an “Experiment,” you enter a prompt or select from the suggested ones, which are quite short. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. extraction.body: YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss. Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows. Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history. YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation. YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery. The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones. Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes. Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts. The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to. Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide. sources.title: Meta Announces Ray-Ban Meta Audio, Its First Smart Glasses Without A Camera - Engadget
passages: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI.

Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature.

extraction.body: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions. Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses ) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display ). The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company. At this moment in Meta's public perception , releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing . The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

extraction.body: Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern. Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making. “Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.” [Image: There are multiple combinations of colors and lenses across two styles for the audio-only glasses. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.” The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too. Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these. Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options. Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.) Why the celebrity collabs? “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.” There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. AI in your frames All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist. “Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel.

extraction.body: At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance. It’s fueled the emergence of camera-free smart glasses challenger brands like Even Realities and Lucyd, and made a large part of the population steer clear of the tech altogether. Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. passages: The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses.

Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras.

Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses.

extraction.body: Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses. From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light, there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists, and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

story.title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses

facts.text: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI.

Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature.
That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes.
Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses.
Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam.
Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables.
These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.) Why the celebrity collabs?
Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed.
Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses.
Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses.

At the center of the privacy backlash against Meta’s AI smart glasses is their in-built camera, which gives wearers a way to covertly film unsuspecting strangers — particularly women — prompting protests against casualized surveillance.

The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299.
On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device.
So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works.

The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it.
“The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts.
A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video.
The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear.
To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light.
Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light.
Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year.
This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data.
Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future.
They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner.
The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses.

Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras.
You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses.
Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses.
From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects.
Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses.
Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside.
Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

extraction.body: Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI. Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions. Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses ) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display ). The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company. At this moment in Meta's public perception , releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing . The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern. Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making. “Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.” [Image: There are multiple combinations of colors and lenses across two styles for the audio-only glasses. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.” The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too. Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these. Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options. Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.) Why the celebrity collabs? “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.” There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. AI in your frames All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist. “Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel.

Yet the Meta AI smart glasses’ in-built camera is central to the tech giant’s vision for ‘superintelligent’ AI assistants that can understand the world like we do. Now, Meta is making a bid for the privacy conscious, by releasing a new pair of AI smart glasses that ditches the camera altogether, and allows wearers to listen hands-free to music and podcasts, take calls that Meta says “capture your voice more clearly than earbuds”, and talk to Meta’s AI assistant. The audio-only glasses’ battery lasts for up to 12 hours on a single charge, and 48 hours more with their included charging case. The new ‘Ray-Ban Meta Audio’ glasses are the lightest smart glasses yet, weighing in at just 43 grams — indistinguishable from ordinary Ray-Ban glasses and available in classic styles — and for the first time, feature no battery, sensors or other technology running through the nose of the glasses. Asked whether the new audio-only glasses are a response to the heated privacy backlash against smart glasses’ in-built cameras, Meta’s VP of wearables Alex Himel says that the Ray-Ban Meta Audios have been in the works since before the backlash reached fever pitch. He also says that the early adopters of Meta’s smart glasses weren’t buying them chiefly for their camera anyway. “We’ve been working on them full force for two years, but we’ve been talking about it for longer than that,” Himel says, speaking ahead of CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s keynote address at Meta Connect. “The most popular feature among our smart glasses wearers has been audio from day one, so phone calls, music, podcasts. And the feature we’re most excited about long-term is having an AI assistant that’s with you all the time. So the audio glasses deliver on those.” Meta has not disclosed whether audio recording for the glasses is in the works. This makes them currently comparable to the functionalities of a pair of headphones or earbuds, as the in-built Meta AI assistant is comparable to the access consumers have through the smartphone they normally pair with their audio tech. The difference here is that these glasses shrink the two devices normally needed (your smartphone plus the earbuds) down to one — and that’s what Meta is betting will convince consumers they’re worth it. The new audio-only glasses will be available to buy from October 13th for $349, cheaper than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 with cameras, which range from $379 to $459, and more than the cheapest version of Meta’s own brand AI glasses released in June, which start at $299. The audio-only glasses were only one part of Zuckerberg’s announcements — elsewhere, Meta seems to be choosing defiance over retreat from AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, despite the cultural backlash. An AI eyewear blitz Zuckerberg also unveiled several new models, styles and features for its Meta AI smart glasses with in-built cameras, representing its biggest expansion of this main category of AI eyewear yet. All the new styles and shapes announced today at Meta Connect mean that by the end of the year, Meta’s AI smart glasses assortment will comprise 100 glasses options across its Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta own brand. Zuckerberg also unveiled a new version of Meta and EssilorLuxottica’s flagship smart glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. The new version is slimmer, with improved battery life and audio, while significantly broadening the number of styles available, including Aviators and Zena, a new cat-eye — another indication that Meta is increasingly treating choice and design as central to taking smart glasses mainstream. Battery life rises to nine hours, versus eight hours for Gen 2, while a new six-microphone array is designed to improve calls and Meta AI voice commands in noisy environments. A customisable action button gives wearers quicker access to Meta AI, while the 12-megapixel camera can shoot 3K video. Meta says Dolby Atmos video capture will arrive later this year. Like previous generations, Gen 3 has an external LED designed to signal to people nearby when its camera is recording. The effectiveness of these indicators has become an increasingly important issue as smart glasses become less visibly distinguishable from conventional eyewear. To address this, Meta introduced an update that closed a loophole allowing users to begin recording before covering the light. Himel tells Vogue Business that Meta has moved to disable accounts that have been found to have posted content made after tampering with this LED light. Rather than radically reinventing the product, Gen 3 appears to be about refining the technology while dramatically increasing the fashion proposition: more silhouettes, more colours and a slimmer design. A big part of people's privacy concerns over Meta's AI smart glasses stem from the fact that all the data that's collected from the glasses is sent to Meta's cloud servers. On Wednesday, Zuckerberg also announced that Meta is working on private processing for smart glasses on-device. This means that Meta won't have access to the wearer's data. Meta will start rolling this out soon for features like live translation first, and will progressively roll it out to more features like media in future. Meta glasses by Blackpink’s Lisa, and another Kylie Jenner style Back in June, Meta released its first pairs of own-brand Meta AI glasses, which don’t rely on the branded EssilorLuxxotica collaboration. These have the same 12MP camera, microphones and Meta AI assistant access as the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. They came in three main frame models — the Adventurer, Fury, and the Starfire edition, which was a collaboration with the first Meta AI glasses celebrity collaborator, Kylie Jenner. The Meta AI glasses span 26 different style combinations of colors, frames, and lenses, but it was the Starfire Kylie frames that broke furthest beyond tech circles — for better and worse.

sources.title: Meta unveils camera-free AI Ray-Bans amid 'pervert glasses' backlash
passages: The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses.

Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras.
You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses.
Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses.
From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects.
Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses.
Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside.
Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

extraction.body: Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses. From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light, there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists, and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants, and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera.

Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

sources.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
passages: That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

extraction.body: Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged. The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same. [Image: Here’s the compute puck. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands. Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers). Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds. Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser. Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio. Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity. The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds. Disclosure: Meta provided lodging for one Road to VR reporter to attend Meta Connect 2026 where information for this article was gathered .

coreStoryFacts.text: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.
That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

It also sounds like the next one will be something a little different.UploadVR reported that Meta's next head-worn VR device might launch in 2026, but it likely won't be a big, bulky VR headset like we're used to seeing from Quest devices.

extraction.body: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price. Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content). On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses , and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames. Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset. Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets. Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.) Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame , the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset. The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of . Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras. Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors ) . But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.
