extraction.body: Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged. The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same. [Image: Here’s the compute puck. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands. Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers). Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds. Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

extraction.body: Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses. Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300. While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here . Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD. In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°). That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable. Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply. Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical. As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup. Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content. While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S. Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard— released earlier this year on Quest —to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more. Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot. When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand. Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there. At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove , courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies , and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking. Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser. Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio. Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity. The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds. Disclosure: Meta provided lodging for one Road to VR reporter to attend Meta Connect 2026 where information for this article was gathered .

story.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses

facts.text: After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight.
Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro.
While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price.

Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses , but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device.
It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras.
Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.

It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear.
You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video.
A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive.
That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them.

The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.
The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge.

Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court.
I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic.
Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too.
I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

passages: It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year.
Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors.
I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse .
More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses.
Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others.
In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect.

Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility.
The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote.
I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem.
Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 .
These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant.

Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

"I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about.

And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point.

Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family.

"It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted.
Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year.
Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors.
I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse .
More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses.
Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others.
In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect.

Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display . There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI. But it's been a while since we've heard anything about the rumored device, sometimes called "Hypernova 2," so Meta could be holding that one back for now. The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect. It also clearly shows a cable, which supports previous reporting that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck. It's also rumored to support hand and eye tracking rather than a dedicated controller. Showing off a new slate of third-party apps for the frames could be a good way to build more excitement for the product even if we don't see updated hardware.

extraction.body: As Meta’s Threads marks its first anniversary on July 6, one thing is clear: the social media platform is far from the 'Twitter killer' it set out to be. Despite amassing 175 million monthly active users, Threads cannot yet boast the same vibrancy as the popular micro-blogging platform, now called X. Nowhere is this more profound than in India, one of the biggest markets for social media platforms.The Meta India team had feared this. In fact, in the lead-up to the launch last year, on July 6, 2023, they had expressed their apprehensions to the Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the Threads' core team, The New Indian Express has learnt. They were not heeded.'Poorly executed'"We were very unhappy with the product -- its viability, the lacklustreness of its functions, and its hurried, overnight launch," said a Meta India insider who was part of the Threads team. The plan was to capitalise on the unrest at Twitter after Elon Musk's takeover and the growing resentment towards some of his proposals, such as the introduction of subscriptions."Indeed. The months prior saw Musk, the new CEO of Twitter, fire most of the employees, rename the platform X, restore previously banned accounts, introduce fees and firewalls, and overhaul the algorithm and content moderation policies. It was a time of much upheaval at Twitter and Zuckerberg hoped to ride this wave."A smart business move, no doubt, but poorly executed," the source added. Though the India team had warned their counterparts in the US, Zuckerberg's instructions were to press on. In addition to the anti-Elon Musk sentiments, the Facebook creator was also likely influenced by his past successes in the sub-continent.A testing groundIndia has always been a testing ground for new digital products. Meta has designed and rolled out several products here before making it available to other countries. Facebook Lite (2015), WhatsApp Pay (2020) and Instagram Reels (2020) are some examples."Of them, the launch of Instagram Reels is noteworthy as it too was deployed in haste, just weeks after the Indian government banned TikTok. It was a big hit, and the subsequent campaign we ran, Made on Reels, helped draw influencers and brands to the platform in droves. It turned Instagram into the company's primary breadwinner," the Meta source said..Social media addiction linked to aggression in kids: Survey. Indeed, the Made on Reels campaign remains one of the biggest that Meta has ever done, rivalled perhaps only by the hoopla around the launch of Threads. "We envisioned a similar success for Threads, but the product we had was simply an upgraded version of Orkut. I deleted the application from my phone after just one week," the source added.A flash in the panThe same turned out to be the case for a majority of the 100 million who downloaded the application in the first week of its launch, only to delete it later. Data from SimilarWeb, a web traffic analytics firm, indicates that the number of Threads users plummeted by 50% within just 24 hours of its launch, and fell to merely 10% of the initial user base by the end of the month, highlighting the fleeting curiosity and subsequent disinterest among users.Most of Threads’ current 175 million monthly active users are made up of flyby traffic from Meta's other applications. No scroll on Instagram is without reminders of Threads' existence."A desperate move," said Baani Grewal, a senior PR professional who downloaded the application out of curiosity last July, but can't seem to get rid of it now as any attempts to delete it also impairs Instagram. The content meted out to users is not very deviant from other Meta-led platforms," she said.Same algorithm, similar facadeEven at the time of launch, there were rumours among the tech community that despite its Twitter-like facade, what actually runs Threads is the same algorithm as Instagram. Baani further added, "There were not enough elements to distinguish it."However, similarity to an existing platform is not a bad thing. In fact, familiarity with usage can sometimes prove advantageous for a fledgling digital product, said Radha Radhakrishnan, the former vice president (marketing and communications) of Global Alliance for Mass Entrepreneurship."But you have to chip away at it to gain an edge. Offer more value than the current major platform," Radha said. However, taking into cognisance that this is indeed the era of snackable content, she added, "I'm not certain if Threads play the game just yet. "For Threads to be successful, it needs a different character. It should be X++, but right now, it is X-."Social media saturationThis was expected, said Srishty Chawla, the co-founder and CEO of One Source, an integrated marketing firm. "I think people got on to Threads for no other purpose but to avoid feeling the FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) and to see what all the hype was about. And when the shine wore off, the new toy was abandoned and we all returned to the comfort of our good ol' X," she said.Srishty also points out that our social media sphere has reached a saturation point. "Threads didn't bring anything new to the table. No problem-solving or added value compared to what was already out there," he said.He further added, "Around 65% of Twitter users are men, unlike the female-dominated scenes on Facebook or Instagram. Convincing these specific users, who've already formed a habit, to switch to a new platform is a real challenge."Meta legacyWhat likely helped Threads win the users it did, according to Sumit, is the fact that it hails from the Meta family. This is also precisely why many, including pundits, are unwilling to dismiss the platform just yet."It's only natural for Meta to throw their weight on Threads. What is after all one year in the life of a digital product? However, it was only a few years ago that it became the go-to platform that it is today," Radha said.Baani too remembers a time when Twitter was not popular. "It was not until the 2014 Lok Sabha elections that Twitter became widely accepted. Until then, not many people were aware of the platform’s potential," she said.However, she is quick to add that Threads, according to her, is not a competitor to Twitter yet.

sources.title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council - The Guardian
passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

extraction.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to address the United Nations Security Council for a meeting about artificial intelligence this week, a U.N. spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue is also set to join, along with Yoshua Bengio, a professor at Université de Montréal who co-chairs the Independent International Scientific Panel of the United Nations on AI, said Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the secretary-general. The meeting is set for Wednesday, according to Bloomberg , which was first to report the news. The U.N. General Assembly in New York this week comes as the debate around AI safety and regulation has reached a boiling point following warnings from researchers about the dire risks to humanity . President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "Many say bigger than the industrial revolution or the internet itself." OpenAI's disclosure in July that its AI models broke out of a testing environment and autonomously hacked into open-source developer platform Hugging Face set off a wave of concerns about the rise of advanced models and how much they can be contained. Since then, Anthropic has also disclosed cyber incidents with its models, and OpenAI has revealed further " concerning model behavior " by autonomous agents. Last week, Google said that its Gemini model hacked into three other companies. — CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. coreStoryFacts.text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are expected to address the United Nations Security Council for a meeting about artificial intelligence this week, a U.N. spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models.
— CNBC's Jim Forkin contributed to this article.

extraction.body: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”

Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards.

Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.

“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry.

Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue is also set to join, along with Yoshua Bengio, a professor at Université de Montréal who co-chairs the Independent International Scientific Panel of the United Nations on AI, said Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the secretary-general. The meeting is set for Wednesday, according to Bloomberg , which was first to report the news. The U.N. General Assembly in New York this week comes as the debate around AI safety and regulation has reached a boiling point following warnings from researchers about the dire risks to humanity . President Donald Trump , who has repeatedly dismissed the warnings as a "hoax" and "scam" over the past week, addressed the assembly on Tuesday and pledged to "encourage" the nascent technology, despite calls from Amodei and Altman to pace the development of advanced models. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said. "Many say bigger than the industrial revolution or the internet itself." OpenAI's disclosure in July that its AI models broke out of a testing environment and autonomously hacked into open-source developer platform Hugging Face set off a wave of concerns about the rise of advanced models and how much they can be contained. Since then, Anthropic has also disclosed cyber incidents with its models, and OpenAI has revealed further " concerning model behavior " by autonomous agents. extraction.body: UNITED NATIONS, Sept 18 (Reuters) – OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN ​General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Friday. The 15-member Security Council is ‌due to meet on Wednesday on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control. “Sam Altman will brief an open ‌UN ​Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson ⁠told Reuters. Altman’s remarks were expected ⁠to focus on the need for international coordination and shared safety standards, as well as steps OpenAI is taking to ensure people globally benefit, the spokesperson said. Diplomats said they also expected high-level presence at the meeting from Anthropic, but that it ​was yet to be confirmed. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Security Council meeting has been convened by France, which is the president of the ⁠body for September, and will be chaired by French ⁠Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot. In a concept note ​for the meeting circulated to council members by France and seen by Reuters, it said: “In ​light of the risk of misuse of this technology for malicious purposes, ‌and drawing on the Council’s existing engagement in this field, France wishes to underline the urgency of action to foster safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence for the benefit of the international community as a whole.” The UN Security Council, which is charged ⁠with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a “runaway horse” and the ⁠United States warned against its ‌use to censor or repress people. Altman has been warning about ⁠the risks well before the current AI boom. In a ​2015 essay ‌titled “Machine Intelligence, part 1”, he said the “development of superhuman machine ​intelligence is probably ⁠the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”. France, in its concept note, said the meeting aimed to allow participants to “present their analysis of the risks linked to loss of control or the use of the latest AI models to develop, facilitate and conduct actions with an impact on international security and peace.” (Reporting by Michelle Nichols and Deepa Seetharaman, ​Editing by Franklin Paul)

passages: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg rejected calls for an industry-wide slowdown in frontier AI development, arguing that trust and alignment will become competitive requirements for successful models.
Meta's approach also links safety to how frontier labs allocate infrastructure.
Zuckerberg said labs should direct a "significant majority" of compute toward serving users rather than pursuing recursive self-improvement, although he did not disclose a target percentage.
Meta's August essay, "The Future is for Everyone," placed this strategy within a broader argument for distributing advanced AI rather than concentrating it among a handful of labs or governments.
Zuckerberg said competing agents aligned with different users would create checks on centralized power.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Zuckerberg's position leaves safety decisions primarily with individual labs, supported by market incentives, liability and outside evaluation.
It also preserves Meta's ability to continue expanding models and infrastructure without waiting for competitors to adopt a common development schedule.
Muse operates in an isolated environment inside Meta's computing infrastructure and asks permission before sensitive actions.
Meta has also subjected the agent to internal testing and agentic red-teaming, while soliciting outside security research through a bug-bounty program.

Meta reported $31.1 billion of capital expenditures in the second quarter and guided to $130 billion to $145 billion for 2026, with investment going toward server capacity, data-center facilities and networking infrastructure.
The company has said capacity will remain tight as demand grows across model training, consumer agents and enterprise products.
Zuckerberg said Meta Superintelligence Labs already uses independent evaluators and advisers in several areas.

sources.title: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse
passages: Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg rejected calls for an industry-wide slowdown in frontier AI development, arguing that trust and alignment will become competitive requirements for successful models.
Meta's approach also links safety to how frontier labs allocate infrastructure.
Zuckerberg said labs should direct a "significant majority" of compute toward serving users rather than pursuing recursive self-improvement, although he did not disclose a target percentage.
Meta's August essay, "The Future is for Everyone," placed this strategy within a broader argument for distributing advanced AI rather than concentrating it among a handful of labs or governments.
Zuckerberg said competing agents aligned with different users would create checks on centralized power.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
8 , offering free access alongside plans costing $20 and $100 per month.
Zuckerberg's position leaves safety decisions primarily with individual labs, supported by market incentives, liability and outside evaluation.
It also preserves Meta's ability to continue expanding models and infrastructure without waiting for competitors to adopt a common development schedule.
Muse operates in an isolated environment inside Meta's computing infrastructure and asks permission before sensitive actions.
Meta has also subjected the agent to internal testing and agentic red-teaming, while soliciting outside security research through a bug-bounty program.

Meta reported $31.1 billion of capital expenditures in the second quarter and guided to $130 billion to $145 billion for 2026, with investment going toward server capacity, data-center facilities and networking infrastructure.
The company has said capacity will remain tight as demand grows across model training, consumer agents and enterprise products.
Zuckerberg said Meta Superintelligence Labs already uses independent evaluators and advisers in several areas.
Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.

Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.

Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.

Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.

Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

facts.text: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg rejected calls for an industry-wide slowdown in frontier AI development, arguing that trust and alignment will become competitive requirements for successful models.
Meta's approach also links safety to how frontier labs allocate infrastructure.
Zuckerberg said labs should direct a "significant majority" of compute toward serving users rather than pursuing recursive self-improvement, although he did not disclose a target percentage.
Meta's August essay, "The Future is for Everyone," placed this strategy within a broader argument for distributing advanced AI rather than concentrating it among a handful of labs or governments.
Zuckerberg said competing agents aligned with different users would create checks on centralized power.

Zuckerberg's position leaves safety decisions primarily with individual labs, supported by market incentives, liability and outside evaluation.
It also preserves Meta's ability to continue expanding models and infrastructure without waiting for competitors to adopt a common development schedule.
Muse operates in an isolated environment inside Meta's computing infrastructure and asks permission before sensitive actions.
Meta has also subjected the agent to internal testing and agentic red-teaming, while soliciting outside security research through a bug-bounty program.

Meta reported $31.1 billion of capital expenditures in the second quarter and guided to $130 billion to $145 billion for 2026, with investment going toward server capacity, data-center facilities and networking infrastructure.
The company has said capacity will remain tight as demand grows across model training, consumer agents and enterprise products.
Zuckerberg said Meta Superintelligence Labs already uses independent evaluators and advisers in several areas.
Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac.
The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details.
This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.
The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work.
Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.
Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address.
Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect.
Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced.
Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too.

Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.
The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars.
At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives.
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.
